sections.title_en: Introduction to the Prohibitions of Avoda Zara
sections.body_en:
In order for Israel to be able to cleave to the One God and draw blessing to themselves and to the whole world, they must distance themselves from any trace of avoda zara (idolatry). Thereby they will be able to absorb the light of God, walk in the ways of God by doing righteousness and justice, understand His Torah and fulfil His mitzvot, settle the land and be fruitful and multiply in it. And blessing will increase in agriculture, in industry, in science, in society and in art, until we merit the coming of our righteous Mashiaḥ, and all the inhabitants of the world will want to walk in the ways of God.

Therefore, in addition to the prohibition of worshipping avoda zara itself, God commanded Israel several prohibitions:

1) To destroy the idols, as it is stated (Devarim 7:25): "The graven images of their gods you shall burn in fire" (above 3:9).

2) Not to derive benefit from avoda zara and from its accessories, its ornaments and its offerings, as will be explained further on in this chapter.

3) Not to vow or swear in the name of avoda zara, as it is stated (Shemot 23:13): "And make no mention of the name of other gods; it shall not be heard from your mouth." This includes not causing gentiles to swear by their idols (below 11:3).

4) In addition to the mitzva to destroy the idols themselves, there is a mitzva to treat them with contempt in order to destroy their name, as it is stated (Devarim 12:3): "And you shall destroy their name from that place." Destroying the name is also accomplished by changing their name to a derogatory one, as it is stated (ibid. 7:26): "You shall utterly detest it and utterly abhor it, for it is a ḥerem (a banned thing)" (below 14:1).

5) Not to take an interest in avoda zara, lest one be enticed after it, as it is stated (Vayikra 19:4): "Do not turn to the idols" (below chapter 13).

6) Not to benefit avoda zara, that is, not to donate to it, and not even to buy something from which a tax is paid for its upkeep (below 11:6).

7) It is also forbidden to bring a gentile's statue into one's house, as it is stated (Devarim 7:26): "And you shall not bring an abomination into your house." The Sages added a prohibition against renting a dwelling to an idol worshipper who customarily brings an idolatrous statue into his house (below 11:9).

8) Even for decoration, the Torah forbade making statues in the image of the attendants in the upper realm, such as angels, and in the lower realm, such as the sun and moon, and in the image of a human being, so that people should not err after them, as it is stated (Shemot 20:19): "You shall not make [gods] with Me" (below 15:1-7).

9) The Sages added a prohibition against Jews doing things that look like avoda zara, because of mar'it ayin (how it appears to onlookers) (below 12:2-3).

In this chapter we will deal with the prohibition of deriving benefit from avoda zara, and in the following chapters the laws of the other safeguards will be explained.

It is a mitzva to destroy the statues of idols, and it is forbidden to derive benefit from them; one who transgresses and benefits from them is liable to lashes. Even if the statue was made of silver or gold, it is forbidden to melt it down and benefit from its silver or gold, as it is stated (Devarim 7:25-26): "The graven images of their gods you shall burn in fire; you shall not covet the silver or gold on them and take it for yourself, lest you be ensnared by it, for it is an abomination to the Lord your God. And you shall not bring an abomination into your house and become a ḥerem like it; you shall utterly detest it and utterly abhor it, for it is a ḥerem." And it is likewise stated (Devarim 13:18): "And nothing of the ḥerem shall cleave to your hand."

The prohibition of benefit includes four categories: 1) the statues of their gods; 2) their accessories, the implements of their worship; 3) their ornaments, their decorations; 4) offerings, the sacrifices offered to them:

1) The statues of their gods are the statues and objects in which, idol worshippers believe, the power of the gods resides, and which have the power to benefit their worshippers. These include statues in the form of a human being or an animal, asherah trees, and all other things in which idol worshippers believe. For example, if an idol worshipper set up a brick and said to it, "You are my god," or bowed down to it, the brick became an idol and is forbidden for benefit.

2) Their accessories are the implements of their worship, that is, the implements with which idol worship is performed, such as censers for burning incense and a knife for slaughtering sacrifices.

3) The ornaments of the idols are the garments with which the statues are clothed, the crown placed on their head, and anything similar. But the garments of the priests who serve them are not considered ornaments of the idols, and are permitted for benefit (Tosafot; Rosh, Avoda Zara 4:1).

4) Offerings, that is, sacrifices offered to the idols, such as animals slaughtered in their honour or foods offered to them (as explained in note 3).

Since it is forbidden to derive benefit from these four categories even after they have been destroyed, they must be destroyed in a manner that makes it impossible to benefit from the material of which they are made. Therefore, if they were made of wood or of other materials that burn, one burns them and scatters their ashes so as not to benefit from them. Even while disposing of them, one must take care not to benefit from the fire in which they are burned. If one baked bread or cooked a dish over a fire of the wood of avoda zara, they are forbidden for benefit (SA YD 142:1, 4). If they were made of metal that does not burn, such as silver and gold, one must grind them and scatter their particles to the wind, or throw them into the sea in a place from which people will not be able to retrieve them, in which case there is no need to grind them (SA YD 146:14; Shakh 13).1

notes_en.en:
The Torah prohibition of deriving benefit from avoda zara and its offerings is derived from several verses. Here I have cited the derivation brought in the Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 7:2; and in Peninei Halakha, Kashrut 29, note 1, regarding wine, the derivation brought in the Ramban (Shemot 34:15-16; glosses on Sefer Ha-mitzvot, negative commandment 194): "And he will invite you and you will eat of his sacrifice. And you will take of his daughters for your sons, and they will go astray…", where the concern about intermarriage is explained, which is the foundation of the prohibitions of [gentile] wine and bishul akum (food cooked by gentiles).
According to the Sages [of the Mishna], avoda zara must be eliminated by grinding it and scattering the particles into the sea, for if one scatters them on land, he would be fertilising the soil and benefiting from it. According to Rabbi Yosei, one may scatter the particles to the wind even though they will scatter over the land. The halakha follows Rabbi Yosei (Avoda Zara 43b; 49a; SA YD 146:14), since one does not intend to benefit from the particles, and the benefit that comes from them is mixed with the benefit from the other materials in the soil, and the halakha is that "where this and that cause it, it is permitted" (Tosafot, Avoda Zara 43b, s.v. "Amru"; below section 7). Similarly, we learn in the Torah that the way to destroy the avoda zara of the asherah tree is by burning, as it is stated (Devarim 12:3): "And you shall burn their asherim in fire," in such a way that its ashes remain on the ground.

sections.title_en: Idols of Wood and Stone That Become Forbidden for Benefit
sections.body_en:
Statues of gentiles become forbidden for benefit from the time the work of making them is completed. But a statue that a Jew made becomes forbidden only from the time he begins to worship it, since Jews in general are repelled by avoda zara, and as long as he has not worshipped the statue there is still a chance that he will repent and not worship it. The accessories and ornaments of avoda zara, even those of gentiles, do not become forbidden until they have been used in worship (Avoda Zara 51b; SA YD 139:1).

Anything in which there is no handiwork of man, that is, which was not made by man but is so by the nature of its creation, is permitted for benefit even though it was worshipped. Therefore, mountains, hills, rivers and springs that were worshipped are permitted for benefit; and likewise mountain stones that broke off by themselves, remained in their place and were worshipped are permitted. If one overlaid a mountain with gold and it was worshipped, only the overlay is forbidden for benefit. Similarly, if one placed a statue on a stone or drew on a stone for the sake of avoda zara, the stone is forbidden as long as the statue or drawing is on it, and after it is removed the stone is permitted. If an idol worshipper built a house for avoda zara, the house becomes forbidden for benefit. If he built an ordinary house and brought a statue into it, as long as the statue is inside, the house is forbidden for benefit; once it is removed, the house is permitted for benefit. If he built an ordinary house and plastered or whitewashed it for the sake of avoda zara, one removes the plaster or the whitewash and the house is permitted (SA YD 145:1-5).

If one planted a tree in order to worship it, the tree is forbidden for benefit, for it is considered something in which there is human handiwork; and this is the asherah, which there is a mitzva to destroy and uproot so that it does not grow again (Avoda Zara 45b; SA YD 146:15). But if one planted an ordinary tree, it is considered something in which there is no human handiwork, and if he afterwards began to worship it, all that grew on it before that is permitted for benefit, and what grows on it from the time he began to worship it is forbidden for benefit. If one bowed down to an animal, it does not become forbidden. If one slaughtered an animal for the sake of avoda zara, it becomes forbidden for benefit, and this is an offering of avoda zara (SA YD 145:6-8).

Included in the prohibition of benefiting from idols is that it is forbidden to sit in the shade of an asherah tree, that is, in the shade of a tree that is worshipped or under which an idol has been placed. Even when the shade of the asherah extends into the public domain it is forbidden to sit under it; and if a public road passes under the shade of the asherah, if there is another road there as short and convenient, one should take the other road. And if there is no other road there as short and convenient, one may go on his way under the shade of the asherah, and he should run there, to show that he has no interest in benefiting from the shade of the asherah (Avoda Zara 48a-b; SA YD 142:9). Even a tree that is not an asherah, but was planted beside the idol to serve as an ornament for the avoda zara, is forbidden for benefit, and it is forbidden to sit in its shade, by the law of the ornaments of avoda zara (SA YD 142:13).

Trees planted in a garden adjacent to a house of avoda zara, since they were not intended to be an ornament for the avoda zara itself, may be benefited from, as may their shade (Ritva). However, when those present there appear to want to draw near to the avoda zara, it is forbidden because of mar'it ayin (below 12:3).2

notes_en.en: It is forbidden to sit in the shade of a statue, but it is permitted to sit in the shade of an idolatrous temple, since the building is an accessory of avoda zara that was built for the sake of what is inside it and not to make shade outside it. However, within the four amot adjacent to its entrance it is forbidden to sit, because there is a mitzva to distance oneself from avoda zara (based on Pesaḥim 26a, Tosafot s.v. "Shani", first answer; Tur in the name of the Ra'avad; the unattributed view in SA YD 142:10). Some say that it is forbidden to benefit even from the shade outside an idolatrous temple, because with avoda zara one must be more stringent (based on the second answer in Tosafot there; the "some say" view in SA there). Even according to the Ritva and the Taz, who hold that an accessory of an accessory is forbidden (below 11, note 9), it is permitted to benefit from a garden adjacent to a house of avoda zara, since it is not considered an ornament of the avoda zara itself (Ritva, Avoda Zara 51b; SA OḤ 649:4; and see O.H. [?], s.v. "Ganot", regarding taking the four species from a tree planted before the avoda zara itself). According to the Ran (Avoda Zara 21a in the Rif pages), one who intends to benefit from the shade of avoda zara transgresses a Torah prohibition, and according to the Mabit (Kiryat Sefer, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 7) it is rabbinic, because shade has no substance.

sections.body_en:
Sacrifices and offerings (takrovot) that were offered to avoda zara are forbidden for benefit forever. And although an idol worshipper can nullify his statues, as well as the statue's accessories and its ornaments, whereby they become permitted for benefit, he cannot nullify the offerings, and they remain forbidden forever (below section 5).

The sacrifices become forbidden for benefit on condition that they were "ke-ein penim" (like the inner service), that is, that a cultic act was performed with them similar to the services that were performed in the Temple. Therefore, idol worshippers who were accustomed, whenever they slaughtered animals for food, to intend that the slaughter be for the sake of the idols—all their meat is forbidden for benefit by the law of an offering, for slaughter is a service "ke-ein penim".3

Those who bring offerings and place them before the idols: if they are like the things that were brought in the Temple, that is, animal meat, fine flours, oils and fruits of the seven species, then even without an additional cultic act, bringing them is considered "ke-ein penim" and they become forbidden for benefit (SA YD 139:3). But other fruits, flowers and candles brought as an offering do not become forbidden for benefit (Ramban, Rashba, Rosh and SA YD 139:3; the Rambam is stringent).4

notes_en.en:
Avoda Zara 51a explains that an offering to avoda zara becomes forbidden on condition that it is "ke-ein penim", that is, that a cultic act was performed with it resembling one of the services in the Temple, such as slaughter, burning, sprinkling the blood or libation (above 3:3). Therefore, if one slaughtered an animal to Merkulis (Mercury), even though this is not its mode of worship, the animal becomes forbidden. On the other hand, if one threw a stone at Merkulis, even though this is its mode of worship and one is liable to death for it, the stone does not become forbidden, because throwing it is not a service "ke-ein penim".
The Amoraim disagreed (ibid. 50b-51a) about the precise definition of "ke-ein penim": according to Rav, even if one broke a stick before avoda zara, it becomes forbidden by the law of an offering, since breaking resembles slaughter (but if one merely "rattled" the stick before the avoda zara, it does not become forbidden). Whereas according to Rabbi Yoḥanan, even if one slaughtered an animal lacking a limb before avoda zara, it does not become forbidden, since such an animal is not offered in the Temple, and this is not "ke-ein penim" (the Tanna'im there further disagreed whether a locust slaughtered for avoda zara becomes forbidden as an offering). The Rishonim disagreed as to whom the halakha follows: according to the Ra'avad, the Meiri and the Hashlama, the halakha follows Rav, and anything with which an act was performed that resembles even somewhat one of the Temple services becomes forbidden by the law of an offering; therefore one who breaks a stick is considered like one who slaughters an animal, and the stick becomes forbidden. On the other hand, according to the Ramban, Rashba, Ritva and Ra'ah, the halakha follows Rabbi Yoḥanan, that only if there is a complete resemblance to the Temple services does it become forbidden by the law of an offering; therefore a stick broken before avoda zara does not become forbidden (however, breaking off something that is brought to the Temple is considered similar to the slaughter that took place in the Temple, and therefore if grapes were harvested for avoda zara they become forbidden). Tosafot have an intermediate approach, according to which there is no dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yoḥanan, and according to both, if the way of worshipping that avoda zara is with a stick or with an animal lacking a limb, then the stick and the animal become forbidden for benefit by breaking or slaughtering; but if it is not the way to worship it with them, they do not become forbidden. This is the view of the Tur and SA (YD 139:3), except that regarding a locust they were stringent that it becomes forbidden even if it is not the way to worship it with a locust (139:4), when the mode of worship of that avoda zara is by slaughtering an animal (Perisha 14).

Offerings brought before the idol: according to the Ri, the Nimukei Yosef and the Ra'ah, they become forbidden only if a cultic act was performed with them, such as burning part of the offering on the altar. But according to the Rashbam in the name of Rashi, the Rashba and the Rosh, one who places an offering before the idol from the things that were brought in the Temple, such as meat, oils, fine flours, water and salt, even if he did not place it on an altar and performed no additional cultic act with it, this is an offering "ke-ein penim". And so it is ruled in the Tur and SA YD 139:3. Fruits of the seven species brought to an idol, like the bikkurim (first fruits) brought to the Temple, are also considered "ke-ein penim" (Ramban and Ritva, Avoda Zara 51a).
The Rashba (Avoda Zara 51b) and the Taz (139:5) wrote that the meat of a wild animal brought as an offering does not become forbidden, since nothing like it is offered on the altar. The Perisha (139:6) was stringent because of its resemblance to the meat of a domestic animal offered on the altar. Accordingly, it seems that he would also forbid other fruits and vegetables because of their resemblance to the bikkurim fruits. But according to most poskim they are not "ke-ein penim", like the meat of a wild animal. Flowers brought as an offering in temples in the East—even the Perisha would agree that they are not "ke-ein penim" and do not become forbidden. However, if a cultic act is performed with them, then their picking is considered like slaughter (as explained in the previous note).
The Rambam (Hilkhot Avoda Zara 7:16) has a different approach, according to which anything brought as an offering to an idol becomes forbidden for benefit even if nothing like it was brought in the Temple; and therefore anything found near avoda zara is forbidden, since presumably it was brought to it as an offering. Accordingly, in his view, candles or flowers brought before the idols are also forbidden for benefit (as explained in the Beit Yosef 139:9-10). However, many Rishonim wrote that candles and wax that gentiles donated to avoda zara are permitted to Jews for benefit after the priests nullify them, since they are considered ornaments of avoda zara, which can be nullified, and not an "offering", since they are not things offered in the Temple (Tosafot, Ramban, Ran, Rosh, Rabbenu Yeruḥam and others; and so it is ruled in SA YD 139:9. According to the Baḥ 6 and the Shakh 3, a ba'al nefesh (scrupulous person) should take the Rambam's view into account).

sections.title_en: Nullification of a Gentile's Avoda Zara
sections.body_en:
A gentile's avoda zara can be nullified by a gentile, and thereby it becomes permitted for benefit, as it is stated (Devarim 7:25): "The graven images of their gods you shall burn in fire; you shall not covet the silver or gold on them and take it for yourself, lest you be ensnared by it." As long as the statues are "their gods", it is forbidden to take them and benefit from them; but if they nullified them, since they are no longer their gods, there is no prohibition of benefit in them (Avoda Zara 52b; Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 8:8).

The nullification is accomplished by an act of an idol-worshipping gentile that damages the statue and thereby expresses decisively that he does not believe in it, for example if he cut off the tip of its ear, or its nose or its finger. Likewise, if he struck it in its face until its form changed, even though he did not remove anything from it, he has nullified it. But if, out of anger at the idol, he spat on the statue, relieved himself on it or dragged it on the floor, it is not nullified, for idol worshippers sometimes did this in their anger, and afterwards were reconciled and returned to worshipping it. Therefore, only an act of actual damage to the body of the statue expresses a decision to nullify it, and removes from it the prohibition of benefit.

Even when the gentile nullified the statue against his will, his nullification is valid, since he understood that he was performing an act that nullifies its status as an idol. However, only a gentile "who knows the nature of avoda zara", that is, one who worships avoda zara, can nullify it. And even if he worships a different idol, since in general he is an idol worshipper, he can nullify them. But a gentile who does not worship idols cannot nullify them. A gentile minor or a mentally incompetent person cannot nullify avoda zara, since he does not understand the meaning of his actions (Avoda Zara 43a; 52b; Rambam 8:9; SA YD 146:5).

If the gentile nullified the statue, its accessories and ornaments are also permitted. However, the offerings that were offered before it remain forbidden forever. If the gentile nullified the idol's implements of worship, only the implements he nullified are permitted, but the statue and its other accessories and ornaments remain forbidden (Avoda Zara 52b; SA YD 139:2; 146:13).

Statues that broke by themselves are forbidden for benefit, since they were not nullified. Likewise, statues and altars whose owners fled because of war are forbidden for benefit. But if their owners could have returned to worship them after the war and did not return to worship them, and likewise statues and implements of worship that were abandoned because over the generations people stopped believing in them, they are nullified and it is permitted to benefit from them (Avoda Zara 53b; SA YD 146:10-11).5 Accordingly, it seems that ancient temples and statues that people stopped worshipping, even though it is not known that they intended to abandon them, are permitted for benefit; for since much time has passed since they were worshipped, the heirs of their worshippers have abandoned them completely and the prohibition has lapsed (see below 12:8 regarding entering these places).

If the gentile sold the statue, whether to a gentile or to a Jew, it is not nullified, for the one who sells it hopes that a buyer will be found for the statue who will worship it (Avoda Zara 53a; SA YD 146:8). If the gentile sold the statue without specification, the money he received for it is forbidden for benefit, for perhaps he intended to use the money for the needs of avoda zara. But if the gentile sold the statue or its accessories in order to use the money for secular purposes, the money he received is permitted (Avoda Zara 64a; SA YD 144:1).6

notes_en.en: If the gentile disgraced the statue in his anger, he has not yet nullified it, as explained above. But if he disgraced it permanently, according to many he has nullified it (Rashba, Ritva, Nimukei Yosef on Avoda Zara 53a; the Meiri is stringent). Similarly, if after reflection he said that he no longer believes in the idol, according to many he has thereby nullified his statue (Ra'aviya, Mordekhai, Agudda, Baḥ. And although the Beit Yosef raised difficulties against them, the Rema 146:7 mentioned them as a "some say" view without citing a dissenting view, and so wrote the Shakh 8 and the Taz 7).

Mishna Avoda Zara 53a: "If one sold it or pledged it (the avoda zara), Rabbi says: he has nullified it; and the Sages say: he has not nullified it." In the Gemara there, the Amoraim disagreed whether their dispute concerns one who sells the statue to a gentile smith, but when the gentile sells the statue to a Jewish smith he assumes that he will melt it down, and therefore he nullifies it; or whether they disagreed even when the gentile sells it to a Jewish smith, and according to the Sages he has not nullified it, because he hopes that he [the smith] will sell the statue to someone who will worship it. According to the Rosh (Avoda Zara 4:2), the Ran (Avoda Zara 24b in the Rif pages), the Nimukei Yosef (Avoda Zara 53a, s.v. "Keitzad"), the Tur (YD 146:8) and others, the halakha follows the Sages according to the stringent view, that even when he sells to a Jewish smith he has not nullified it, and the statue is forbidden for benefit. And according to the Rambam (Hilkhot Avoda Zara 8:10), the Semag (negative commandments 45), the Kol Bo (97) and others, the halakha follows the Sages according to the lenient view, that if he sold the statue to a Jewish smith he has nullified it and it is permitted for benefit. The SA and the Levush (146:8) ruled without attribution stringently like the Rosh and those who follow him, and cited the Rambam's view as a "some say" view.
According to Tosafot (Avoda Zara 53a, s.v. "Aval"), for those who are lenient and hold that a sale to a Jewish smith nullifies it, the same law applies if he sold it to a Jew who is not a smith. And many Rishonim inferred this to be Rashi's view (ibid., s.v. "Stam"). On the other hand, according to the Rambam (Hilkhot Avoda Zara 8:10), the Ramban in the name of the Ra'avad, the Rashba, the Ritva (Avoda Zara 53a) and others, only if he sold it to a Jewish smith has he nullified it, but not to an ordinary Jew, for the Jewish buyer knows that the value of avoda zara is higher than that of ordinary metal, and therefore the seller hopes that the Jew will sell the statue to a gentile and will not melt it down.
The nullification of an altar is accomplished by demolishing most of it, as it is stated (Yeshayahu 27:9): "When he makes all the stones of the altar like chalkstones that are crushed, asherim and sun-images shall rise no more"; thus only when all the stones of the altar have been crushed does it no longer have any standing, and the majority is like the whole (Avoda Zara 53b-54a, Ra'avad and Tosafot Rid there; Rambam 8:12; Levush 146:12. According to the Kiryat Sefer, by Torah law it suffices to crush any amount, and by rabbinic law most of it must be broken). The Rambam wrote that the altar must be "demolished for the most part by gentiles". The Beit Yosef (146:12) explained that otherwise the prohibition of benefit remains, like avoda zara that broke by itself. And so wrote the SA 146:12, and the Aḥaronim there (Levush, Shakh, Gra and others). Some hold that the Rambam does not mean that gentiles specifically must break it, but that the altar must be broken while it is still in the hands of the gentiles, before it passes into the hands of a Jew (Ḥiddushei Ha-Rim; Yad Peshuta).
In contrast to the Rambam and those who agree with him, the Rashba explained (Avoda Zara 54a, s.v. "Ha") that even by demolishing any amount, the altar is permitted, like the nullification of a statue, and only if it was destroyed by itself must most of it be destroyed. And so wrote the students of Rabbenu Yona (cited in Kovetz Shitot Kamai, Avoda Zara 53b).

sections.title_en: A Jew's Avoda Zara Can Never Be Nullified
sections.body_en:
A Jew's avoda zara can never be nullified, for from the moment the Jew began to worship it there is a Torah obligation to destroy it, and consequently it is forbidden for benefit forever. And what we learned, that a gentile's avoda zara can be nullified, is because there is no obligation upon the gentile to destroy the avoda zara; consequently, if he nullifies it, it is nullified, and thereby its material becomes permitted (SA YD 146:1). The accessories and ornaments of a Jew's avoda zara likewise are not nullified, for there is an obligation to destroy them, and consequently there is no possibility of nullifying them and thereby permitting them (Gra 146:2). Even a Jewish apostate who is devoted to avoda zara cannot nullify avoda zara (Taz 139:1).

If a Jew sold avoda zara or its accessories, the money he received in exchange for them is also forbidden for benefit; and likewise if he exchanged them for something else, such as an animal, the animal also becomes forbidden for benefit, as it is stated (Devarim 7:25-26): "The graven images of their gods you shall burn in fire… And you shall not bring an abomination into your house and become a ḥerem like it": whatever you receive for it will be forbidden for benefit like it (Avoda Zara 54b; SA YD 144:1; 145:9).

The Sages decreed that even a gentile's avoda zara that came into the possession of a Jew, since it became his, he is obligated to destroy it, and there is no possibility of its being nullified by a gentile; lest, if people are lenient with it, they come to be lenient also with a Jew's avoda zara, which cannot be nullified (Semag; SA YD 146:1-2).7

notes_en.en: Avoda Zara 64b: "A Jew who found an idol in the marketplace: before it comes into his hand, he may tell a gentile to nullify it; once it has come into his hand, he may not tell a gentile to nullify it." That is to say, even if he did not acquire it, since it came into his possession, it can never be nullified (Baḥ and Shakh 146:1). However, the accessories and ornaments of avoda zara, as long as a Jew has not acquired them, can be nullified (SA YD 146:2). According to most Rishonim, this law, that avoda zara that came into a Jew's possession can never be nullified, is a rabbinic decree, lest people come to permit benefit through nullification even of avoda zara belonging to a Jew, whereas by Torah law it can be nullified (Semag, negative commandments 45; Ramban and Ritva, Avoda Zara 53b; Yere'im 102; Beit Yosef YD 146:2; Levush 2; Taz 3, and many others). On the other hand, it emerges from Rashi (Avoda Zara 42a, s.v. "Ein") that this law is from the Torah, and is derived from "and sets it up in secret" (Devarim 27:15). It is also implied by the Rambam (Hilkhot Avoda Zara 8:9) that it is from the Torah, since he equated a Jew's avoda zara with avoda zara that came into a Jew's hands (so wrote many regarding his view: Mekor Mayim Ḥayim YD 146:2; the Netziv in Harḥev Davar on Devarim 12:3, who explained that the prohibition is derived from "The graven images of their gods you shall burn in fire").

sections.title_en: The Prohibition of Mixtures of Avoda Zara
sections.body_en:
Because of the severity of the prohibition of avoda zara, the Sages ordained that avoda zara is not nullified even in a thousand: if an idolatrous statue became mixed with similar statues made for decoration and not for worship, all are forbidden for benefit. If a spoon that was used for idolatrous worship became mixed with ordinary spoons, all are forbidden for benefit. And likewise if a piece of meat that was offered to avoda zara became mixed with a thousand pieces, all are forbidden for benefit (Avoda Zara 74a; Rambam, Hilkhot Avoda Zara 7:9; SA YD 140:1).

As we have learned (in section 2), it is forbidden to benefit from things of avoda zara; but when it is not a matter of an actual mixture of avoda zara, but only of something that was caused by avoda zara, the rule is "zeh ve-zeh gorem, mutar" (where this and that cause it, it is permitted). That is to say, when two factors contributed to the creation of something, one forbidden and one permitted, the resulting product is permitted. Therefore, although it is forbidden to feed an animal vegetables that were offered as an offering to avoda zara, and it is forbidden to fertilise a field with an offering to avoda zara, if an animal was fed an offering, it is permitted to eat its meat or drink its milk, because they were created through a combination of permitted and forbidden foods. And if a field was fertilised with an offering to avoda zara, it is permitted to sow in the field, since the field was enriched by permitted fertilisers that accumulated in it naturally and also by fertiliser of avoda zara (Avoda Zara 49a; SA YD 142:11; see Peninei Halakha, Kashrut 34:6; Pesaḥ 8:5, note 6).

sections.title_en: Benefit from the Music, Scent and Sight of Avoda Zara
sections.body_en:
It is forbidden to enjoy hearing songs and melodies that are sung or played for avoda zara, and likewise it is forbidden to enjoy seeing the images of avoda zara or smelling the incense burned to it (Rabbenu Yeruḥam 17:5; SA YD 108:7; 142:15). And one who turns himself to enjoy them or gaze at them transgresses a Torah prohibition, as it is stated (Vayikra 19:4): "Do not turn to the idols" (Shabbat 149a; below 13:1).

One who needs to pass on his way near a place of worship at a time when the scent of incense being burned there rises from it, or when the sound of singing or music being sung or played before the avoda zara is heard from it, or in a place where he sees its ornaments, may pass on condition that he does not intend to benefit from it, and also that it is not inevitable that he will benefit from it; for example, if a desire to enjoy it arises in him, he can block his nose so as not to smell, or stop his ears so as not to hear, or turn his gaze so as not to see. In that case, as long as he does not intend to benefit, even if he smells, hears or sees, he is permitted to pass. But if he cannot avoid smelling, hearing or seeing, then even if he does not intend to benefit, he is forbidden to pass there. All the more so it is forbidden for him to pass there when he intends to benefit (Rabbenu Yeruḥam ibid.; Shakh 142:34). The law of enjoying music and pictures that were recorded or photographed in a place of worship will be explained below (13:8).8

notes_en.en:
In Pesaḥim 26a, it was said regarding the Temple that sound and sight "are not subject to me'ila (misuse of consecrated property) (for they have no substance). Me'ila does not apply, but a prohibition does apply"; and with scent there is also me'ila if its mitzva has not been performed. Rabbenu Yeruḥam (Toledot Adam Ve-ḥava 17:5) learned from this that it is forbidden to benefit from the scent, sound and sight of avoda zara. Likewise in Avoda Zara 12b, according to Reish Lakish, it is forbidden to buy in shops decorated with roses and myrtle that are offerings to avoda zara, "because he benefits from the scent… for the verse says: And nothing of the ḥerem shall cleave to your hand" (and so Rashi there 13a, s.v. "Nehene"). And so it is ruled in SA YD 142:15; Shakh 32. And so wrote the Shiyurei Berakha 142:2, that from the words of the SA one should learn an explicit prohibition against entering houses of avoda zara to see their ornaments.
The Rishonim asked regarding Reish Lakish: surely the buyer does not intend to smell. And they explained that since he lingers there, there is a concern that he will intend to benefit (Ra'avad, Ramban, Rashba, Ritva, Ran, Meiri and others). They further asked: surely it is accepted that "scent is nothing", so why is it forbidden? Many explained that with something designated for scent, such as rose and myrtle, scent is something, and it is forbidden (Rashba, Ritva, Ran, Meiri, Roke'aḥ and others). And some say that because of the severity of avoda zara, one is stringent even with scent emanating from something not intended for scent (Rash of Sens. And some say in the name of the Ri that the scent in which there is no prohibition is a scent that harms the one who smells it).
From the plain sense of the Gemara in Pesaḥim 26a, it emerges that benefit from the scent of hekdesh (consecrated property) is forbidden by Torah law, whereas benefit from sight and sound is rabbinic; and so wrote Rashi there, the Semag (positive commandments 210), and so it is implied by the Rambam (Hilkhot Me'ila 5:16). Rabbenu Yeruḥam (Toledot Adam Ve-ḥava 17:5) equated the law of avoda zara with hekdesh, and he was cited by the Beit Yosef and SA YD 142:15; and the Rosh Yosef (Pesaḥim ibid.) explained that regarding avoda zara too, the prohibition of scent is by Torah law and the prohibition of sound and sight is rabbinic. And so it emerges from Torat Mordekhai (128b), Rav Yitzḥak Antebi (Beit Av on Rambam, Hilkhot Shabbat 1:5), and the Penei Yehoshua (Pesaḥim 25b). And see Biur Halakha (217:7, s.v. "Ve-im rov"). Some hold that regarding avoda zara, sound and sight are also forbidden by Torah law (Ḥatam Sofer, Ḥullin 89a); and on the other hand, some wrote that regarding avoda zara even scent is forbidden only rabbinically (Tosafot Yeshanim, Yoma 60a; Ḥokhmat Ha-Torah by Rav Shlomo Kluger, Vayetze p. 396).
Benefit that comes to a person against his will: from the discussion in Pesaḥim 26a, it emerges that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon, that if one does not intend to benefit, it is permitted to walk on a road where he will smell, see or hear avoda zara even when he has another road. All the more so it is permitted to walk on it when he has no other road, that is: "it is impossible [to avoid it] and he does not intend." Tosafot added (25b, s.v. "Lo efshar") that even according to Rabbi Shimon, in a case of pesik reisha (an inevitable consequence) it is forbidden. The Rosh explained (Pesaḥim 2:2) that the permission is "for example where he can block his nostrils so as not to benefit from the scent", and then even if he does not block his nostrils it is permitted. But if he cannot block his nose, then even if he does not intend to benefit, since it is a pesik reisha that by walking there he will smell the incense of avoda zara, it is forbidden. And so wrote Rabbenu Yeruḥam (Toledot Adam Ve-ḥava 17:5). And so wrote the Shakh 142:34 in practice. (His words are explained in the Ḥafetz Ḥayim, rule 6, gloss on Be'er Mayim Ḥayim, subsection 14.) On the other hand, according to the Ran (Ḥullin 32a in the Rif pages), if one does not intend to benefit, even in a pesik reisha that he will benefit, it is permitted, because with prohibitions of benefit one follows the intention, and if he does not intend to benefit, the benefit that comes to him against his will is not considered benefit. And so it appears from the glosses of the Riaz on the Shiltei Ha-gibborim.

sections.title_en: Performing Mitzvot with Things of Avoda Zara
sections.body_en:
All things that did not become forbidden for benefit even though they were worshipped, such as things in which there is no human handiwork, like stones and animals (above section 3), or that were nullified by gentiles (above section 5), since they were worshipped, became repulsive and disqualified for the Temple service (Arukh Ha-shulḥan He-atid, Hilkhot Issurei Mizbe'aḥ 55:20). Therefore, if one bowed down to his animal, it is disqualified as a sacrifice, and priestly garments are not made from its wool. If one bowed down to mountain stones, they are disqualified for building the altar. If one bowed down to a spring that flows in his courtyard, all the water that was in it at that time is disqualified for the water libation. And likewise an asherah tree that gentiles worshipped and afterwards nullified—logs of wood are not brought from it for the altar (Rambam, Hilkhot Issurei Mizbe'aḥ 4:7).

The Rishonim disagreed whether these things are also forbidden for other mitzvot, such as for a shofar, a lulav and tzitzit. In practice it is ruled that even if they belonged to a gentile and he nullified them, so that they are permitted for benefit, they have become repulsive for a mitzva, and le-khatḥila (ab initio) one should not use them for the needs of a mitzva.

Be-di'avad (after the fact), if one used them for a mitzva, the law depends on whether they can be nullified or not. If they belong to a Jew, he has not fulfilled the mitzva, for since there is an obligation to destroy them from the world, they are considered as if destroyed, and consequently it is impossible to fulfil a mitzva with them. But if they belong to a gentile, since they can be nullified they are not considered as if destroyed; and even though in practice they were not nullified and are therefore forbidden for benefit, be-di'avad he has fulfilled his obligation of performing the mitzva with them, because performing mitzvot is not considered benefit.9

notes_en.en:
Avoda Zara 47a: "Reish Lakish asked: if one bowed down to a palm tree, what is the law regarding its lulav for a mitzva?" And the doubt remained unresolved ("teiku"). In the Gemara, Sukka 31b, it is explained that one does not fulfil the obligation with a lulav from an "asherah of Moshe" (an asherah that Israel found upon entering the Land), because it is considered eliminated and destroyed, and therefore even be-di'avad one does not fulfil the obligation with it. But with a lulav of avoda zara one does fulfil the obligation. And the same is explained in Rosh Hashana 28a regarding a shofar of avoda zara. The Rishonim disagreed in explaining the difference between an "asherah of Moshe" and ordinary avoda zara. Three opinions were stated: 1) According to the lenient opinion, an "asherah of Moshe" is a Jew's avoda zara, which cannot be nullified and must be destroyed, and therefore one does not fulfil the obligation with it. But a gentile's avoda zara, as long as it has not been nullified, le-khatḥila one should not perform a mitzva with it, but if one did, he has fulfilled it; and if he nullified it, one may le-khatḥila perform a mitzva with it (Ran, Sukka 14a in the Rif pages, s.v. "Shel asheira"). 2) According to the stringent opinion, an "asherah of Moshe" is a gentile's avoda zara that he did not nullify, and its law is that even be-di'avad one does not fulfil the obligation with it; and if he nullified it, one fulfils the obligation be-di'avad (Rabbenu Tam in Tosafot, Sukka 31b, s.v. "Asheira"). 3) According to the intermediate opinion, an "asherah of Moshe" is a Jew's avoda zara, and even be-di'avad one does not fulfil the obligation, for it is as if eliminated. And with a gentile's avoda zara, if he did not nullify it, one fulfils the obligation be-di'avad, because "mitzvot were not given for benefit". And if he nullified it, Reish Lakish in the Gemara, Avoda Zara 47a, was in doubt whether it is permitted to perform a mitzva with it le-khatḥila, and the doubt remained unresolved (Tosafot, Avoda Zara 47a, s.v. "Mi ma'is"; Rashi, Ḥullin 89a, s.v. "Lo im"). And since it is a doubt, one should be stringent (Mordekhai, Avoda Zara 843, in the name of the Ra'aviya; Rabbenu Yeruḥam, Toledot Adam Ve-ḥava 17:4; cited by the Beit Yosef YD 139:13). And so it is ruled in the SA (OḤ 586:3 regarding a shofar; 649:3 regarding a lulav; YD 139:13 regarding Shabbat and Ḥanuka candles; Magen Avraham 586:6, explaining SA 11:8, regarding tzitzit). The MB (586:18) wrote that if one has only a shofar of avoda zara that has not been nullified, he should blow it, because the main halakhic view is that be-di'avad one fulfils the obligation; but if afterwards another shofar becomes available to him, he should blow it without a berakha, in order to take into account the view of the stringent authorities. And for the altar, according to all opinions they are disqualified (below, note 11).
In continuation of this, the Responsa Re'em 81 (by Rabbi Eliyahu Mizraḥi) wrote that it is permitted to benefit from a garment that priests wore when they served avoda zara, but one should not make a tallit for a mitzva from it, because it is repulsive. And so wrote the SA YD 139:13. However, the Re'em there permitted entering a synagogue with a garment that had belonged to priests.

sections.title_en: Converting a Church into a Synagogue
sections.body_en:
The poskim disagreed whether it is permitted to convert a church that has been nullified into a synagogue. Some forbid it, because after the building was used for the needs of avoda zara, it became repulsive for the needs of a mitzva. Indeed, by being sold for any use, it is no longer considered an accessory of avoda zara, and it is permitted to benefit from it; but just as it is forbidden to light in a synagogue candles that were used for avoda zara, even if they were nullified from serving it (SA OḤ 154:11), so it is forbidden to make a synagogue out of a building that served as a church and was nullified (Eliyahu Rabba 154:15).

Some say that it is permitted to convert a church into a synagogue, for only movable things that were used for avoda zara become repulsive for a mitzva, but a building attached to the ground does not become repulsive. In addition, it was not the building itself that was worshipped, and therefore from the time it ceased to serve avoda zara, it is permitted to convert it into a synagogue (Magen Avraham 154:17).

In practice, le-khatḥila one should be stringent not to make a synagogue out of a building that served as a church, and be-di'avad, if it was done, one may pray in it.10

notes_en.en:
From Responsa Re'em 81 it emerges that it is permitted to pray in a building in which there was previously avoda zara, just as it is customary to pray in a place that previously belonged to gentiles in which they regularly worshipped images. However, in SA OḤ 154:11 he forbade using in a synagogue candles that had previously served avoda zara. The Magen Avraham (154:17) explained that the Re'em permitted it because the prohibition of using avoda zara for the needs of a mitzva does not apply to something attached to the ground. In addition, it was not the building itself that was worshipped. Those who agreed with him: Ḥokhmat Adam 84:15; Ein Yitzḥak vol. 1, OḤ 10; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 154:15. On the other hand, the Eliyahu Rabba (154:15) was stringent, and so wrote Sha'arei Tzedek OḤ 12 (by Rav Panet); Maharam Schick YD 154; Zikhron Yehuda 66. According to Responsa Binyan Tziyon 63, even if the building was not originally built to be a church, in a time of need one may rely on the lenient authorities, but le-khatḥila one should not make it a synagogue (and so wrote Tzitz Eliezer 12:15:7 regarding the Re'em's view). Some permitted it only in a Protestant church, since it has no statues (Sho'el U-meshiv, first edition 3:72; MB 154:45; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 82). In practice, the custom has been to be lenient with all kinds of churches, as the MB wrote (154:45), and so was the custom in the United States, as cited in Igrot Moshe OḤ 1:49. In practice, le-khatḥila one should be stringent, and if a synagogue has already been made from a building that served as a church, one should not refrain from praying in it. And so wrote Igrot Moshe OḤ 1:49, that the law of repulsiveness for a mitzva applies only le-khatḥila, and therefore be-di'avad, if a large sum has already been paid and a synagogue made from a church, one may pray in it le-khatḥila. And he wrote that if the church burned down and needs renovation, and the building will have a new appearance, it is permitted. [See Megilla 6a, on the verse (Zekharia 9:7): "And I will remove his blood from his mouth and his abominations from between his teeth, and he too shall remain for our God, and he shall be like a chief in Yehuda, and Ekron like a Jebusite," which plainly implies that at the time of the redemption houses of avoda zara will be converted into synagogues and study halls. On the other hand, Tosafot there, s.v. "Teratriyot", wrote that this is impossible, but rather they will be desolate, and the Gemara's intention is that the meeting houses of idol worshippers will be converted into synagogues; and so wrote the Dagul Me-revava on OḤ 154.]
Chairs and benches: the Shevet Sofer 12 permitted buying chairs that were in a church for the use of a synagogue, and so wrote the MB 154:46 based on the Pri Megadim, adding that they do not require nullification, since they are made only for sitting and not as ornaments of avoda zara. Lamps: the MB wrote there that they are considered ornaments of avoda zara, and therefore lamps that were in a church and that a Jew took after the gentile nullified them, although they are permitted for ordinary use, are forbidden for a synagogue because they are repulsive (based on the Pri Megadim in explanation of the Taz, and Rabbi Akiva Eiger; unlike the Eliyahu Rabba, who permitted it).

sections.title_en: Candles and Decorations Manufactured for Avoda Zara
sections.body_en:
If one designates an animal to be sacrificed to avoda zara, then from the time a preparatory act is performed with it, for example if the priests shore its wool in honour of the idol, even if the owner of the animal changes his mind and no longer wishes to sacrifice it to avoda zara, it is forbidden to be offered on the altar to God.

However, all this applies specifically to offering on the altar, because it is repulsive to offer before God in the Temple an animal that was designated to be sacrificed to avoda zara. But it is permitted to use candles that were designated to be lit before the idol for lighting Shabbat or Ḥanuka candles. Similarly, it is permitted to decorate the sukka with decorations that were manufactured for decorating avoda zara and churches.11

notes_en.en:
An animal that was set aside for avoda zara is disqualified for the altar (Temura 29a; Bekhorot 57a; Bava Kamma 40b). And although the general rule is that "designation is nothing", that is, designating an object for the needs of a mitzva does not sanctify it until the designation is actually carried out with it—for example, if a garment was designated as a shroud for a dead person, it does not become forbidden for other uses until the dead person is actually wrapped in it—with regard to avoda zara the law is more severe: once an animal has been designated for avoda zara through a preparatory act, it is forbidden to be offered on the altar to God. But as long as the designation was made only verbally, it does not become forbidden, for it was said in the Tosefta (Temura 4:2-3): "There is no consecration for avoda zara." And likewise it was said in the baraita in Temura 29a: "A set-aside animal is forbidden only once an act has been done with it," for example if the sheep's wool was shorn. And so ruled the Rambam (Hilkhot Issurei Mizbe'aḥ 4:4), Bartenura (Temura 6:1) and others. On the other hand, the Ra'avad (in his glosses on the Rambam there) had a different version of the Gemara in Temura there, according to which the animal becomes forbidden by the very act of setting it aside verbally for the idol, and once the priests perform an act with it that cancels its designation for avoda zara, such as shearing its wool, it is permitted to be offered on the altar. Rashi (Temura 29a, s.v. "Ad") and Tosafot (ibid., s.v. "Ela") adopted this version.
The Parashat Ha-kesef (Hilkhot Avoda Zara 7:2) wrote that although there would be room to say that le-khatḥila one should not light, in the synagogue, on Shabbat or on Ḥanuka, a candle that was set aside to serve before avoda zara, in practice one may be lenient for several reasons: 1) According to the Rambam's approach, the animal becomes forbidden for the altar only when a cultic act was performed with it, such as shearing its wool; but here, where the candles were merely manufactured for this purpose, they are permitted. 2) Even according to the Ra'avad's approach that no act is necessary, it is possible that setting aside for avoda zara forbids only offering on the altar and not other mitzvot. Similarly ruled the Ikarei Ha-dat 8:38; Ḥatam Sofer OḤ 42; MB 154:44, and others. 3) Even according to the Ra'avad, it is possible that selling the candles to a Jew is considered a nullification, whereby the priests have nullified the candles from serving before avoda zara, and the prohibition has lapsed from them.

sections.title_en: Wigs Whose Hair Comes from India
sections.body_en:
In 5764 (2004), a controversy arose concerning wigs whose hair is brought from India. It became clear that some of the hair is brought from the area of the city of Tirupati in southern India, where there is a place of worship visited by tens of millions of people a year, many of whom shave the hair of their heads in preparation for coming before the idol. The hair belonging to the place of worship is afterwards sold to the global wig industry. Those who forbade argued that shaving the hair is a cultic act, and is consequently considered like slaughter, whereby the hair becomes forbidden for benefit. And although the Rishonim disagreed whether in such a case the hair becomes forbidden, those who forbade ruled according to the stringent view. On the other hand, those who permitted inquired of people familiar with their religion, and it became clear that the shaving is not a cultic act but only a preparation for coming before the idol in submission, and consequently, according to all opinions, the hair does not become forbidden for benefit.

In practice, even if we take into account the view of the stringent authorities, since there are two doubts in this law, even when it is known that the wig's hair was brought from Tirupati, the wig is permitted. All the more so when the source of the hair is not known, for then there are three doubts, as explained in the note.12

notes_en.en:
The first doubt: whether shaving the hair is a cultic act or only a preparation for coming before the idol. From the investigations of the matter, it appears that the lenient authorities are correct, for the priests of that religion themselves said that the shaving is not worship, and that the hair is considered impure in their eyes and unfit for an offering; and laypeople said the same. With this the discussion should have ended. Nevertheless, the stringent authorities persisted in arguing that many laypeople think the shaving is worship, and therefore it is considered the mode of worship of that idol, whereby the hair becomes forbidden.
The second doubt: even if we accept the view of the stringent authorities that cutting the hair is worship, we learned above in note 3 that the Rishonim disagreed whether the hair becomes forbidden thereby: according to the Ramban, Rashba and Ritva, only worship that resembles the Temple service forbids the offering, and consequently here, where it does not resemble it, it is permitted. And according to the Ra'avad, Tosafot and SA YD 139:3, as long as it is the mode of worship with that thing, if the mode of worship somewhat resembles the Temple service, the thing becomes forbidden for benefit, and consequently here, where cutting the hair resembles slaughter, the hair becomes forbidden. In practice, regarding the prohibition of benefit from avoda zara, in a case of sfek sfeka (a double doubt) the halakha follows the lenient authorities (Shakh 141:7). Therefore, even when it is known that the wig's hair is from Tirupati, the wig is permitted.
The third doubt concerns the laws of mixtures: according to the lenient authorities, a minority of the hair brought to the wig industry comes from India, and a minority of the hair brought from India comes from Tirupati. Therefore, although the Sages were stringent that the prohibition of avoda zara is not nullified even in a thousand, here, where the hair brought from Tirupati is mixed two and three times in different places, and each time it is a minority, it is thereby nullified (SA YD 140:1. Admittedly, according to SA YD 108:10 the permission applies only in a third mixture, but the Rema wrote that with a doubtful prohibition the permission applies in a second mixture. According to the Levush, in any case the permission applies in a second mixture, and according to the Shakh 110:50, in a case of great financial loss one may be lenient in a second mixture). Even if there is a doubt whether in all the mixtures the hair from Tirupati was a minority, it is a rabbinic doubt, whose law is to be lenient, since overall the hair from Tirupati is nullified in a majority by Torah law. On the other hand, the stringent authorities argue that the hair brought from there is considered "kavua" (fixed in place), and there are not two stages here but a single mixing of the hair from the place of worship with the rest of the hair in the whole world.
Although according to the three doubts it should be permitted, the spokesmen of the stringent authorities behaved as "ba'alei maḥloket" (contentious people), and disparaged and dismissed the view of the lenient authorities, and wrote anonymous scurrilous pamphlets against them; and according to the lenient authorities, they even prevented them from presenting their arguments before the elderly rabbis in whose name they had forbidden it.
